title: More Collaboration Makes You Slower: The Counterintuitive Management Method of the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
dek: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.
why: High information density, but the second half is worth more than the first. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.
who: Product leaders, startup founders, engineering and design managers currently wrestling with collaboration and decision-making efficiency.
skip: The opening introduction and the Ustream reminiscences can be skipped; the ad mechanics and management principles in the middle and back half are the most valuable.

points.h: More collaboration makes the system slower
points.body: Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating,’ and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why you are doing this thing, plus a very clear organizational structure that specifies who can be trusted to make which decision. With those two things, you don't need to over-collaborate and you still get results that look ‘as if you had collaborated.’

points.h: The median PM gap is a mathematical structure problem
points.body: Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail; once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power-law distribution is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have an extremely strong incentive to stay; meanwhile the truly strong ones have skills that fit almost perfectly into other executive roles or starting their own company, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system.’ Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into whatever shape they want, and especially bad engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

points.h: There are three mathematical reasons Snap's ads can't scale
points.body: First, users are extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuity’ in ad CPMs in and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what is hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising runs on a screen that shows ads, whereas Snap opens a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there is no logical place to put an ad; it is a creation-oriented product, not a consumption-oriented one. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited over and over, but break it down by ‘dollars spent per unit of time’ and none of them does particularly well.

points.h: Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
points.body: Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to better ideas than almost anything any other consumer startup has ever shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what is currently on display in the product is only a small part of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judges suitable for this time and place. He offers a way to probe taste in an interview: ask the person about something they built but never shipped — not something killed because the data tested badly, but something they held as a prototype and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready.’ If a museum hung its entire collection on the walls, the curator would have done nothing.

points.h: Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
points.body: Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in advertising — Meta already solved the modern ad auction, this ‘solved problem,’ from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component quickly. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: it isn't the highest bidder who wins, but rather the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so whoever bids high has to pay more to reach people who don't want to be reached. This mechanism lets organic content and ad content go into the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

points.h: In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
points.body: Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy,’ and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced one — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you are willing to trade away. He uses Amazon search as an example: search for something and you have to scroll past 16 ads before you see the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor isn't whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is very likely correlated with user retention, and may even be causal.

points.h: Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
points.body: Snap and Discord both confirmed it twice: network-effect businesses want to grow on their own, and the most effective move is to serve the people already using the product, or wanting to use it for its actual job, better — faster, more relevant. He explains it with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly active users to equal one daily active user, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio; moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter in Snap's overall DAU history that went flat quarter over quarter; after that the team ground away at Android performance, producing a growth revival that lasted years. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord, and outsiders all thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up Discord's usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney segment.

points.h: SpaceX is burning its own ships by hand
points.body: Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most worth learning from is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and yet SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and move to Starship. He calls this a Cortez-level burning of the ships, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing, you are still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also mentions that SpaceX and Tesla publish ten-year plans openly on their websites, and Tesla even opens its patents; that confidence — ‘I'll tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

points.h: Long-term greedy: using ideology as cover for long-termism
points.body: One phrase Peter used repeatedly on the ad teams at Snap and Discord is long-term greedy. Behind it is math: tomorrow's ad revenue is causally linked to the ROI you create for advertisers today, so the focus should be on advertiser ROI. The hard part is that the easiest way to improve ROI is to lower the denominator — just cut prices — and in a modern auction price is an output, not an input. What he really means is this: in any career there will be moments when long-termism is extremely painful, like a public company missing its numbers and possibly having to lay people off, and at those moments you need a set of ideology as ‘cover’ that gives you room to make long-term decisions — we're not doing charity, we're giving up margin today because we know they'll come back tomorrow with a bigger budget.

points.h: Core product value takes seven years of repeating it weekly
points.body: Peter says Snap's core product value was not a slogan on the wall, but an onboarding presentation he personally gave to every new employee, every week or every other week, for seven straight years. His logic: with only metrics and no story, data scientists and engineers won't act on it every day; with only a story and no metrics, nobody knows what to optimize. So you must have both, and repeat them — part of what he calls the ‘cult’: this is how we deliver core product value, this is why people still choose Snapchat every day in the face of a mass of substitutes and a pack of ferocious competitors.

points.h: A great PM is three pairs of wolves fighting each other
points.body: Peter thinks great PM is itself an oxymoron, specifically three contradictions: first, extremely confident to the point of arrogance, alongside genuinely serious humility, able to accurately credit the designer who changed the design at the last second and the engineer who pulled an all-nighter for a partner event; second, extremely organized and respectful of process, while also extremely tolerant of ambiguity, even near-pathologically averse to authority — ‘I have a checklist for everything, but I can also throw it away and redo it at any moment’; third, long-term thinking coexisting with a near-annoying bias to action; a great PM can set the cadence for the whole company — ‘he wakes up in the morning, and the team is awake.’

points.h: Some consumer product ability can't be learned
points.body: Peter's spiciest take: to build truly great consumer products for certain specific groups, the PMs and designers on those products need certain inalienable traits that cannot be learned or acquired — he explicitly lists gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic background. He stresses this is not the simple mapping of ‘building a product for young Black men means hiring young Black men,’ but rather that most consumer products are essentially playing to certain parts of Maslow's hierarchy, and people with certain upbringings and physical conditions understand those needs better. He also admits this is in many cases not even executable, which is exactly why it's the spicy take.
